300A.title: Guillemet
300A.description: Double chevrons used as quotation marks
300A.extract: Guillemets are a pair of punctuation marks in the form of sideways double chevrons, « and », sometimes used as quotation marks or ditto marks. When used as quotation marks, single guillemets, ‹ and ›, are used for nested quotations. Guillemets are not conventionally used in English.

300B.title: Guillemet
300B.description: Double chevrons used as quotation marks
300B.extract: Guillemets are a pair of punctuation marks in the form of sideways double chevrons, « and », sometimes used as quotation marks or ditto marks. When used as quotation marks, single guillemets, ‹ and ›, are used for nested quotations. Guillemets are not conventionally used in English.

301C.title: Wave dash
301C.description: East Asian character primarily used to represent a range
301C.extract: Wave dash (U+301C 〜 WAVE DASH) is a character represented in Japanese character encoding mainly used as a dash and chōonpu. The wave dash is similar to, but not the same as, the tilde character (U+FF5E ～ FULLWIDTH TILDE), which is often used interchangeably with it.

304A.title: O (kana)
304A.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
304A.extract: O (hiragana: お, katakana: オ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, they occupy the fifth place in the modern Gojūon (五十音) system of collating kana. In the Iroha, they occupy the 27th, between の and く. In the table at right (ordered by columns, from right to left), お lies in the first column (あ行, "column A") and the fifth row (お段, "row O"). Both represent [o].

304B.title: Ka (kana)
304B.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
304B.extract: Ka (hiragana: か, katakana: カ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ka]. The shapes of these kana both originate from 加.

304C.title: Ka (kana)
304C.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
304C.extract: Ka (hiragana: か, katakana: カ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ka]. The shapes of these kana both originate from 加.

304D.title: Ki (kana)
304D.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
304D.extract: Ki (hiragana: き, katakana: キ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ki] and are derived from a simplification of the 幾 kanji. The hiragana character き, like さ, is drawn with the lower line either connected or disconnected.

304E.title: Ki (kana)
304E.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
304E.extract: Ki (hiragana: き, katakana: キ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ki] and are derived from a simplification of the 幾 kanji. The hiragana character き, like さ, is drawn with the lower line either connected or disconnected.

304F.title: Ku (kana)
304F.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
304F.extract: Ku (hiragana: く, katakana: ク) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [kɯ] and their shapes come from the kanji 久.

305B.title: Se (kana)
305B.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
305B.extract: Se (hiragana: せ, katakana: セ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent the sound [se], and when written with dakuten represent the sound [ze]. In the Ainu language, the katakana セ is sometimes written with a handakuten (which can be entered into a computer as either one character (セ゚) or two combined ones (セ゜) to represent the [t͡se] sound, and is interchangeable with ツェ (tse).

305D.title: So (kana)
305D.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
305D.extract: So (hiragana: そ, katakana: ソ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent [so]. Besides the one-stroke form of this kana used by computer fonts, many native Japanese writers use a different form in handwriting, here listed as an alternative form.

305F.title: Ta (kana)
305F.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
305F.extract: Ta (hiragana: た, katakana: タ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ta]. た originates from the Chinese character 太, while タ originates from 多.

306A.title: Na (kana)
306A.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
306A.extract: Na (hiragana: な, katakana: ナ) are Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana な is made in four strokes, the katakana ナ two. Both represent [na]. な and ナ originate from the man'yōgana 奈. な is used as part of the okurigana for the plain negative forms of Japanese verbs, and several negative forms of adjectives.

306B.title: Ni (kana)
306B.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
306B.extract: Ni (hiragana: に, katakana: ニ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is written in three strokes, while the katakana in two. Both represent /ni/ although for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [ɲi].

306C.title: Nu (kana)
306C.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
306C.extract: Nu (hiragana: ぬ, katakana: ヌ) is one of the Japanese kana each representing one mora. Both hiragana and katakana are made in two strokes and represent [nɯ]. They are both derived from the Chinese character 奴. In the Ainu language, katakana ヌ can be written as small ㇴ to represent a final n, and is interchangeable with the standard katakana ン.

306D.title: Ne (kana)
306D.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
306D.extract: Ne (hiragana: ね, katakana: ネ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is made in two strokes, while the katakana is made in four. Both represent [ne].

306E.title: No (kana)
306E.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
306E.extract: No (hiragana: の, katakana: ノ) are Japanese kana, both representing one mora. In the gojūon system of ordering of Japanese morae, it occupies the 25th position, between ね (ne) and は (ha). It occupies the 26th position in the iroha ordering. Both represent the sound [no]. The katakana form is written similar to the Kangxi radical 丿, radical 4.

306F.title: Ha (kana)
306F.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
306F.extract: Ha (hiragana: は, katakana: ハ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represent one mora. Both represent [ha]. They are also used as a grammatical particle (in such cases, they denote [wa], including in the greeting "konnichi wa") and serve as the topic marker of the sentence. は originates from 波 and ハ from 八.

307B.title: Ho (kana)
307B.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
307B.extract: Ho (hiragana: ほ, katakana: ホ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are made in four strokes and both represent [ho]. In the Sakhalin dialect of the Ainu language, ホ can be written as small ㇹ to represent a final h sound after an o sound (オㇹ oh).

307E.title: Ma (kana)
307E.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
307E.extract: Ma (hiragana: ま, katakana: マ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is made in three strokes, while the katakana in two. Both represent [ma]. The characters ま and マ are respectively based on the sōsho style and simplification of the kanji 末.

307F.title: Mi (kana)
307F.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
307F.extract: Mi (hiragana: み, katakana: ミ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in two strokes, while the katakana is made in three. Both represent [mi].

308A.title: Ri (kana)
308A.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
308A.extract: Ri (hiragana: り, katakana: リ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are written with two strokes and both represent the sound [ɾi] . Both originate from the character 利. The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇼ to represent a final r sound after an i sound (イㇼ ir).

308B.title: Ru (kana)
308B.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
308B.extract: Ru (hiragana: る, katakana: ル) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represent one mora. The hiragana is written in one stroke; the katakana in two. Both represent the sound [ɾɯ] . The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇽ to represent a final r sound after an u sound (ウㇽ ur).

308C.title: Re (kana)
308C.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
308C.extract: Re (hiragana: れ, katakana: レ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in two strokes, while katakana in one. Both represent the sound [ɾe] . The shapes of these kana have origins in the character 礼. The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇾ to represent a final r sound after an e sound (エㇾ er).

308D.title: Ro (kana)
308D.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
308D.extract: Ro (hiragana: ろ, katakana: ロ) (romanised as ro) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in one stroke, katakana in three. Both represent [ɾo] and both originate from the Chinese character 呂. The Ainu language uses a small ㇿ to represent a final r sound after an o sound (オㇿ or).

308F.title: Wa (kana)
308F.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
308F.extract: Wa (hiragana: わ, katakana: ワ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. It represents [wa] and has origins in the character 和. There is also a small ゎ/ヮ, that is used to write the morae /kwa/ and /gwa/ (くゎ, ぐゎ), which are almost obsolete in contemporary standard Japanese but still exist in the Ryukyuan languages. A few loanwords such as shīkwāsā (シークヮーサー; from Okinawan language) and Musica Antiqua Köln (ムジカ・アンティクヮ・ケルン, Mujika Antikwa Kerun; a German early music group) contain this kana in Japanese. Katakana ワ is also sometimes written with dakuten, ヷ, to represent a /va/ sound in foreign words; however, most IMEs lack a convenient way to write this.

309A.title: Dakuten and handakuten
309A.extract: The dakuten (Japanese: 濁点; Japanese pronunciation: [dä̀.kɯ̥̈.té̞ɴ̀, -.té̞ɴ́],) voicing mark, lit. 'muddying mark', colloquially ten-ten (点々, 'dots'), is a diacritic most often used in the Japanese kana syllabaries to indicate that the consonant of a mora should be pronounced as voiced — for instance, on sounds that have undergone rendaku (sequential voicing).

309B.title: Dakuten and handakuten
309B.extract: The dakuten (Japanese: 濁点; Japanese pronunciation: [dä̀.kɯ̥̈.té̞ɴ̀, -.té̞ɴ́],) voicing mark, lit. 'muddying mark', colloquially ten-ten (点々, 'dots'), is a diacritic most often used in the Japanese kana syllabaries to indicate that the consonant of a mora should be pronounced as voiced — for instance, on sounds that have undergone rendaku (sequential voicing).

309F.title: Yori (kana)
309F.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
309F.extract: Yori (hiragana: ゟ, katakana: ) is one of the Japanese kana. It is a polysyllabic kana which represents two morae. Both the hiragana and katakana forms represent [joɾi] "from". ゟ is a combination (ligature) of the hiragana graphs of yo (よ) and ri (り), while is a combination (ligature) of the katakana graphs of yo (ヨ) and ri (リ).

30A0.title: Double hyphen
30A0.extract: In Latin script, the double hyphen ⹀ is a punctuation mark that consists of two parallel hyphens (‐). It was a development of the earlier double oblique hyphen ⸗, which developed from a Central European variant of the virgule slash, originally a form of scratch comma. Similar marks (see below) are used in other scripts.

30A2.title: A (kana)
30A2.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30A2.extract: A (hiragana: あ, katakana: ア) is a Japanese kana that represents the mora consisting of single vowel [a]. The hiragana character あ is based on the sōsho style of kanji 安, while the katakana ア is from the radical of kanji 阿. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, it occupies the first position of the alphabet, before い. Additionally, it is the 36th letter in Iroha, after て, before さ. The Unicode for あ is U+3042, and the Unicode for ア is U+30A2.

30A4.title: I (kana)
30A4.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30A4.extract: I (い in hiragana or イ in katakana) is one of the Japanese kana each of which represents one mora. い is based on the sōsho style of the kanji character 以, and イ is from the radical (left part) of the kanji character 伊. In the modern Japanese system of sound order, it occupies the second position of the mora chart, between あ and う. Additionally, it is the first letter in Iroha, before ろ. Both represent the sound [i]. In the Ainu language, katakana イ is written as y in their Latin-based mora chart, and a small ィ after another katakana represents a diphthong.

30A6.title: U (kana)
30A6.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30A6.extract: U (hiragana: う, katakana: ウ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, they occupy the third place in the modern Gojūon (五十音) system of collating kana. In the Iroha, they occupied the 24th position, between む and ゐ. In the Gojūon chart (ordered by columns, from right to left), う lies in the first column (あ行, "column A") and the third row (う段, "row U"). Both represent the sound [ɯ]. In the Ainu language, the small katakana ゥ represents a diphthong, and is written as w in the Latin alphabet.

30A8.title: E (kana)
30A8.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30A8.extract: E (hiragana: え, katakana: エ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, they occupy the fourth place in the modern Gojūon (五十音) system of collating kana. In the Iroha, they occupy the 34th, between こ and て. In the table at right (ordered by columns, from right to left), え lies in the first column (あ行, "column A") and the fourth row (え段, "row E"). Both represent [e].

30AA.title: O (kana)
30AA.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30AA.extract: O (hiragana: お, katakana: オ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, they occupy the fifth place in the modern Gojūon (五十音) system of collating kana. In the Iroha, they occupy the 27th, between の and く. In the table at right (ordered by columns, from right to left), お lies in the first column (あ行, "column A") and the fifth row (お段, "row O"). Both represent [o].

30AB.title: Ka (kana)
30AB.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30AB.extract: Ka (hiragana: か, katakana: カ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ka]. The shapes of these kana both originate from 加.

30AC.title: Ka (kana)
30AC.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30AC.extract: Ka (hiragana: か, katakana: カ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ka]. The shapes of these kana both originate from 加.

30AD.title: Ki (kana)
30AD.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30AD.extract: Ki (hiragana: き, katakana: キ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ki] and are derived from a simplification of the 幾 kanji. The hiragana character き, like さ, is drawn with the lower line either connected or disconnected.

30AE.title: Ki (kana)
30AE.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30AE.extract: Ki (hiragana: き, katakana: キ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ki] and are derived from a simplification of the 幾 kanji. The hiragana character き, like さ, is drawn with the lower line either connected or disconnected.

30AF.title: Ku (kana)
30AF.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30AF.extract: Ku (hiragana: く, katakana: ク) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [kɯ] and their shapes come from the kanji 久.

30B1.title: Ke (kana)
30B1.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30B1.extract: Ke (hiragana: け, katakana: ケ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent [ke]. The shape of these kana come from the kanji 計 and 介, respectively.

30B3.title: Ko (kana)
30B3.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30B3.extract: Ko (hiragana: こ, katakana: コ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent IPA: [ko]. The shape of these kana comes from the kanji 己.

30B5.title: Sa (kana)
30B5.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30B5.extract: Sa (hiragana: さ, katakana: サ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [sa]. The shapes of these kana originate from 左 and 散, respectively.

30B7.title: Shi (kana)
30B7.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30B7.extract: Shi (hiragana: し, katakana: シ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent the phonemes /si/, reflected in the Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki romanization si, although for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [ɕi] , which is reflected in the Hepburn romanization shi. The shapes of these kana have origins in the character 之. The katakana form has become increasingly popular as an emoticon in the Western world due to its resemblance to a smiling face.

30BD.title: So (kana)
30BD.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30BD.extract: So (hiragana: そ, katakana: ソ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent [so]. Besides the one-stroke form of this kana used by computer fonts, many native Japanese writers use a different form in handwriting, here listed as an alternative form.

30BF.title: Ta (kana)
30BF.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30BF.extract: Ta (hiragana: た, katakana: タ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ta]. た originates from the Chinese character 太, while タ originates from 多.

30C1.title: Chi (kana)
30C1.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30C1.extract: Chi (hiragana: ち, katakana: チ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both are phonemically /ti/, reflected in the Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki romanization ti, although, for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [t͡ɕi] , which is reflected in the Hepburn romanization chi.

30C4.title: Tsu (kana)
30C4.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30C4.extract: Tsu (hiragana: つ, katakana: ツ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are phonemically /tɯ/, reflected in the Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki Romanization tu, although for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [t͡sɯᵝ] , reflected in the Hepburn romanization tsu.

30C6.title: Te (kana)
30C6.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30C6.extract: Te (hiragana: て, katakana: テ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent [te].

30C8.title: To (kana)
30C8.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30C8.extract: To (hiragana: と, katakana: ト) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent the sound [to], and when written with dakuten represent the sound [do]. In the Ainu language, the katakana ト can be written with a handakuten (which can be entered in a computer as either one character (ト゚) or two combined characters (ト゜) to represent the sound [tu], and is interchangeable with the katakana ツ゚.

30CA.title: Na (kana)
30CA.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30CA.extract: Na (hiragana: な, katakana: ナ) are Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana な is made in four strokes, the katakana ナ two. Both represent [na]. な and ナ originate from the man'yōgana 奈. な is used as part of the okurigana for the plain negative forms of Japanese verbs, and several negative forms of adjectives.

30CB.title: Ni (kana)
30CB.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30CB.extract: Ni (hiragana: に, katakana: ニ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is written in three strokes, while the katakana in two. Both represent /ni/ although for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [ɲi].

30CC.title: Nu (kana)
30CC.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30CC.extract: Nu (hiragana: ぬ, katakana: ヌ) is one of the Japanese kana each representing one mora. Both hiragana and katakana are made in two strokes and represent [nɯ]. They are both derived from the Chinese character 奴. In the Ainu language, katakana ヌ can be written as small ㇴ to represent a final n, and is interchangeable with the standard katakana ン.

30CD.title: Ne (kana)
30CD.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30CD.extract: Ne (hiragana: ね, katakana: ネ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is made in two strokes, while the katakana is made in four. Both represent [ne].

30CE.title: No (kana)
30CE.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30CE.extract: No (hiragana: の, katakana: ノ) are Japanese kana, both representing one mora. In the gojūon system of ordering of Japanese morae, it occupies the 25th position, between ね (ne) and は (ha). It occupies the 26th position in the iroha ordering. Both represent the sound [no]. The katakana form is written similar to the Kangxi radical 丿, radical 4.

30CF.title: Ha (kana)
30CF.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30CF.extract: Ha (hiragana: は, katakana: ハ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represent one mora. Both represent [ha]. They are also used as a grammatical particle (in such cases, they denote [wa], including in the greeting "konnichi wa") and serve as the topic marker of the sentence. は originates from 波 and ハ from 八.

30D5.title: Fu (kana)
30D5.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30D5.extract: Fu (hiragana: ふ, katakana: フ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is made in four strokes, while the katakana in one. It represents the phoneme /hɯ/, although for phonological reasons (general scheme for /h/ group, whose only phonologic survivor to /f/ ([ɸ]) remaining is ふ: b←p←f→h), the actual pronunciation is [ɸɯᵝ] , which is why it is romanized fu in Hepburn romanization instead of hu as in Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki rōmaji (Korean 후 /hu/ creates the same phonetic effect as lips are projected when pronouncing "u"). Written with a dakuten (ぶ, ブ), they both represent a "bu" sound, and written with handakuten (ぷ, プ) they both represent a "pu" sound.

30D8.title: He (kana)
30D8.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30D8.extract: He (hiragana: へ, katakana: ヘ) is one of the Japanese kana, which represents one mora. The [he] sound is the only sound that is written almost identically in hiragana and katakana and therefore confusable according to the Unicode Standard. In the Sakhalin dialect of the Ainu language, ヘ can be written as small ㇸ to represent a final [h] after an [e] sound (エㇸ [eh]).

30DB.title: Ho (kana)
30DB.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30DB.extract: Ho (hiragana: ほ, katakana: ホ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are made in four strokes and both represent [ho]. In the Sakhalin dialect of the Ainu language, ホ can be written as small ㇹ to represent a final h sound after an o sound (オㇹ oh).

30DE.title: Ma (kana)
30DE.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30DE.extract: Ma (hiragana: ま, katakana: マ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is made in three strokes, while the katakana in two. Both represent [ma]. The characters ま and マ are respectively based on the sōsho style and simplification of the kanji 末.

30E0.title: Mu (kana)
30E0.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30E0.extract: Mu (hiragana: む, katakana: ム) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is written with three strokes, while the katakana is written with two. Both represent [mɯ].

30E1.title: Me (kana)
30E1.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30E1.extract: Me (hiragana: め, katakana: メ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both versions of the kana are written in two strokes and represent [me].

30E2.title: Mo (kana)
30E2.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30E2.extract: Mo (hiragana: も, katakana: モ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are made in three strokes and both represent [mo].

30E4.title: Ya (kana)
30E4.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30E4.extract: Ya (hiragana: や, katakana: ヤ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in three strokes, while the katakana is written in two. Both represent [ja]. Their shapes have origins in the character 也.

30E6.title: Yu (kana)
30E6.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30E6.extract: Yu (hiragana: ゆ, katakana: ユ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represents one mora. Both the hiragana and katakana forms are written in two strokes and represent the sound [jɯ]. The hiragana character ゆ is based on the sōsho style of the kanji 由, while the katakana ユ is based on a simplification of the kanji 弓.

30E8.title: Yo (kana)
30E8.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30E8.extract: Yo (hiragana: よ, katakana: ヨ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is made in two strokes, while the katakana in three. Both represent [jo].

30E9.title: Ra (kana)
30E9.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30E9.extract: Ra (hiragana: ら; katakana: ラ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both versions are written with two strokes and have origins in the character 良; both characters represent the sound [ɾa] . The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇻ to represent a final r sound after an a sound (アㇻ ar).

30EA.title: Ri (kana)
30EA.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30EA.extract: Ri (hiragana: り, katakana: リ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are written with two strokes and both represent the sound [ɾi] . Both originate from the character 利. The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇼ to represent a final r sound after an i sound (イㇼ ir).

30EB.title: Ru (kana)
30EB.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30EB.extract: Ru (hiragana: る, katakana: ル) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represent one mora. The hiragana is written in one stroke; the katakana in two. Both represent the sound [ɾɯ] . The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇽ to represent a final r sound after an u sound (ウㇽ ur).

30EC.title: Re (kana)
30EC.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30EC.extract: Re (hiragana: れ, katakana: レ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in two strokes, while katakana in one. Both represent the sound [ɾe] . The shapes of these kana have origins in the character 礼. The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇾ to represent a final r sound after an e sound (エㇾ er).

30ED.title: Ro (kana)
30ED.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30ED.extract: Ro (hiragana: ろ, katakana: ロ) (romanised as ro) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in one stroke, katakana in three. Both represent [ɾo] and both originate from the Chinese character 呂. The Ainu language uses a small ㇿ to represent a final r sound after an o sound (オㇿ or).

30F0.title: Wi (kana)
30F0.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30F0.extract: Wi (hiragana: ゐ, katakana: ヰ) is an obsolete kana (Japanese phonetic character) that is normally pronounced [i] (the same as the kana for i) in current-day Japanese.

30F1.title: We (kana)
30F1.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30F1.extract: We (hiragana: ゑ, katakana: ヱ) is an obsolete kana (Japanese phonetic character) that is pronounced [e] (same pronunciation as e (kana): え) in current-day Japanese.

30F2.title: Wo (kana)
30F2.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30F2.extract: Wo (hiragana: を, katakana: ヲ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Historically, both are phonemically /wo/, reflected in the Nihon-shiki wo, although the contemporary pronunciation is [o] , reflected in the Hepburn romanization and Kunrei-shiki romanization o. Thus it is pronounced identically to the kana o. Despite this phonemic merger, the kana wo is sometimes regarded as a distinct phoneme from /o/, represented as /wo/, to account for historical pronunciation and for orthographic purposes.

30F3.title: N (kana)
30F3.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30F3.extract: N (hiragana: ん, katakana: ン) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. ん is the only kana that does not end in a vowel sound (although in certain cases the vowel ending of kana, such as す, is unpronounced). The kana for mu, む/ム, was originally used for the n sound as well, while ん was originally a hentaigana used for both n and mu. In the 1900 Japanese script reforms, hentaigana were officially declared obsolete and ん was officially declared a kana to represent the n sound.

30F6.title: Small ke
30F6.description: Small form of the Japanese character ke
30F6.extract: The small ke (ヶ) is a Japanese character, typographically a small form of the katakana character ケ ke.

30FC.title: Chōonpu
30FC.extract: The chōonpu (Japanese: 長音符; lit. "long sound symbol"), also known as chōonkigō (長音記号), onbiki (音引き), bōbiki (棒引き), or Katakana-Hiragana Prolonged Sound Mark by the Unicode Consortium, is a Japanese symbol that indicates a chōon, or a long vowel of two morae in length. Its form is a horizontal or vertical line in the center of the text with the width of one kanji or kana character. It is written horizontally in horizontal text and vertically in vertical text (ー). The chōonpu is usually used to indicate a long vowel sound in katakana writing and rarely in hiragana writing. The chōonpu is a distinct mark from the dash, and in most Japanese typefaces it can easily be distinguished.

30FF.title: Koto (kana)
30FF.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
30FF.extract: Koto (hiragana: , katakana: ヿ) is one of the Japanese kana. It is a polysyllabic kana which represents two morae. Both the hiragana and katakana forms represent [koto]. is a combination (ligature) of the hiragana graphs of ko (こ) and to (と), while ヿ originates from the Chinese character 事.

314A.title: Chieut
314A.description: Consonant letter of the Korean Hangul alphabet
314A.extract: Chieut (letter: ㅊ; name: 치읓) is a consonant of the Korean hangul alphabet. Its IPA pronunciation is [tʃʰ] but at the end of a syllable it is pronounced [t] unless followed by a vowel. For example: 김치 kimchi, but 꽃 kkot ("flower").

314B.title: Kieuk
314B.description: Consonant letter of the Korean alphabet
314B.extract: Kieuk (letter: ㅋ; name: 키읔) is a consonant of the Korean Hangul alphabet. It is pronounced aspirated, as [kʰ] at the beginning of a syllable and as [k] at the end of a syllable. For example: 코 ko ("nose") is pronounced [kho], while 부엌 bueok ("kitchen") is pronounced [puʌk].

314C.title: Tieut
314C.extract: Tieut (letter: ㅌ; name: 티읕) is a consonant of the Korean hangul alphabet. It is pronounced aspirated, as [tʰ] at the beginning of a syllable and as [t] at the end of a syllable. For example: 토마토 tomato [tʰomatʰo] but 붙다 butta ("to stick to"), where it is pronounced with an unaspirated [t] sound.

314D.title: Pieup
314D.description: Consonant letter of the Korean Hangul alphabet
314D.extract: Pieup (letter: ㅍ; name: 피읖) is a consonant of the Korean hangul alphabet. It is pronounced aspirated, as [pʰ] at the beginning of a syllable and as [p] at the end of a syllable. For example: aspirated in 프랑스 peurangseu ("France"), but unaspirated in 앞 ap ("front"). In loanwords, this jamo is used when transliterating "f" in 필름 pilleum ("film").

314E.title: Hieut
314E.description: Consonant letter of the Korean alphabet
314E.extract: Hieut (letter: ㅎ; name: 히읗) is a consonant letter (jamo) of the Korean Hangeul alphabet. It has two pronunciation forms, [h] at the beginning of a syllable and [t̚] at the end of a syllable. After vowels or the consonant ㄴ it is semi-silent.

314F.title: A (hangul)
314F.description: Vowel letter of the Korean Hangul alphabet
314F.extract: A (letter: ㅏ; name: 아) is a jamo, the smallest component of the Korean hangul writing system. It represents a vowel, the IPA pronunciation of which is [a].

315E.title: We (hangul)
315E.description: Letter of the Korean Hangul alphabet
315E.extract: We (letter: ㅞ; name: 웨) is one of the Korean hangul.

317F.title: Bansiot
317F.description: Archaic letter of the Korean alphabet Hangul
317F.extract: Bansiot (letter: ㅿ; name: 반시옷), sometimes called samgakhyeong (삼각형; lit. 'triangle'), is an archaic consonant letter of the Korean alphabet, Hangul. In Unicode, its name is spelled pansios, following the ISO/TR 11941 romanization system. Bansiot's sound value is disputed, but most scholars believe it to have been the voiced alveolar fricative [z] in Middle Korean. It fell out of use around the late 16th century, as its corresponding phoneme disappeared from the language.

318D.title: Araea (letter)
318D.description: Archaic letter of the Korean alphabet Hangul
318D.extract: Araea (letter: ㆍ; name: 아래아) is an archaic vowel letter of the Korean alphabet, Hangul. It was associated with either an open-mid back unrounded vowel ([ʌ]), an open back rounded vowel ([ɒ]), or an open-mid back rounded vowel ([ɔ]). While the letter is no longer used in modern Hangul orthographies for the Korean language, it is used for the Jeju language.

31D9.title: Yi (kana)
31D9.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
31D9.extract: Yi (hiragana: 𛀆, katakana: 𛄠) is a Japanese mora or a kana used to write it, though it has never been in standard use.

320A.title: Kieuk
320A.description: Consonant letter of the Korean alphabet
320A.extract: Kieuk (letter: ㅋ; name: 키읔) is a consonant of the Korean Hangul alphabet. It is pronounced aspirated, as [kʰ] at the beginning of a syllable and as [k] at the end of a syllable. For example: 코 ko ("nose") is pronounced [kho], while 부엌 bueok ("kitchen") is pronounced [puʌk].

320B.title: Tieut
320B.extract: Tieut (letter: ㅌ; name: 티읕) is a consonant of the Korean hangul alphabet. It is pronounced aspirated, as [tʰ] at the beginning of a syllable and as [t] at the end of a syllable. For example: 토마토 tomato [tʰomatʰo] but 붙다 butta ("to stick to"), where it is pronounced with an unaspirated [t] sound.

320C.title: Pieup
320C.description: Consonant letter of the Korean Hangul alphabet
320C.extract: Pieup (letter: ㅍ; name: 피읖) is a consonant of the Korean hangul alphabet. It is pronounced aspirated, as [pʰ] at the beginning of a syllable and as [p] at the end of a syllable. For example: aspirated in 프랑스 peurangseu ("France"), but unaspirated in 앞 ap ("front"). In loanwords, this jamo is used when transliterating "f" in 필름 pilleum ("film").

320D.description: Consonant letter of the Korean alphabet
320D.extract: Hieut (letter: ㅎ; name: 히읗) is a consonant letter (jamo) of the Korean Hangeul alphabet. It has two pronunciation forms, [h] at the beginning of a syllable and [t̚] at the end of a syllable. After vowels or the consonant ㄴ it is semi-silent.

326A.description: Consonant letter of the Korean alphabet
326A.extract: Kieuk (letter: ㅋ; name: 키읔) is a consonant of the Korean Hangul alphabet. It is pronounced aspirated, as [kʰ] at the beginning of a syllable and as [k] at the end of a syllable. For example: 코 ko ("nose") is pronounced [kho], while 부엌 bueok ("kitchen") is pronounced [puʌk].

326C.description: Consonant letter of the Korean Hangul alphabet

326D.description: Consonant letter of the Korean alphabet

32D0.title: A (kana)
32D0.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D0.extract: A (hiragana: あ, katakana: ア) is a Japanese kana that represents the mora consisting of single vowel [a]. The hiragana character あ is based on the sōsho style of kanji 安, while the katakana ア is from the radical of kanji 阿. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, it occupies the first position of the alphabet, before い. Additionally, it is the 36th letter in Iroha, after て, before さ. The Unicode for あ is U+3042, and the Unicode for ア is U+30A2.

32D1.title: I (kana)
32D1.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D1.extract: I (い in hiragana or イ in katakana) is one of the Japanese kana each of which represents one mora. い is based on the sōsho style of the kanji character 以, and イ is from the radical (left part) of the kanji character 伊. In the modern Japanese system of sound order, it occupies the second position of the mora chart, between あ and う. Additionally, it is the first letter in Iroha, before ろ. Both represent the sound [i]. In the Ainu language, katakana イ is written as y in their Latin-based mora chart, and a small ィ after another katakana represents a diphthong.

32D2.title: U (kana)
32D2.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D2.extract: U (hiragana: う, katakana: ウ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, they occupy the third place in the modern Gojūon (五十音) system of collating kana. In the Iroha, they occupied the 24th position, between む and ゐ. In the Gojūon chart (ordered by columns, from right to left), う lies in the first column (あ行, "column A") and the third row (う段, "row U"). Both represent the sound [ɯ]. In the Ainu language, the small katakana ゥ represents a diphthong, and is written as w in the Latin alphabet.

32D3.title: E (kana)
32D3.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D3.extract: E (hiragana: え, katakana: エ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, they occupy the fourth place in the modern Gojūon (五十音) system of collating kana. In the Iroha, they occupy the 34th, between こ and て. In the table at right (ordered by columns, from right to left), え lies in the first column (あ行, "column A") and the fourth row (え段, "row E"). Both represent [e].

32D4.title: O (kana)
32D4.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D4.extract: O (hiragana: お, katakana: オ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. In the modern Japanese system of alphabetical order, they occupy the fifth place in the modern Gojūon (五十音) system of collating kana. In the Iroha, they occupy the 27th, between の and く. In the table at right (ordered by columns, from right to left), お lies in the first column (あ行, "column A") and the fifth row (お段, "row O"). Both represent [o].

32D5.title: Ka (kana)
32D5.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D5.extract: Ka (hiragana: か, katakana: カ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ka]. The shapes of these kana both originate from 加.

32D6.title: Ki (kana)
32D6.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D6.extract: Ki (hiragana: き, katakana: キ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ki] and are derived from a simplification of the 幾 kanji. The hiragana character き, like さ, is drawn with the lower line either connected or disconnected.

32D7.title: Ku (kana)
32D7.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D7.extract: Ku (hiragana: く, katakana: ク) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [kɯ] and their shapes come from the kanji 久.

32D8.title: Ke (kana)
32D8.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D8.extract: Ke (hiragana: け, katakana: ケ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent [ke]. The shape of these kana come from the kanji 計 and 介, respectively.

32D9.title: Ko (kana)
32D9.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32D9.extract: Ko (hiragana: こ, katakana: コ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent IPA: [ko]. The shape of these kana comes from the kanji 己.

32DA.title: Sa (kana)
32DA.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32DA.extract: Sa (hiragana: さ, katakana: サ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [sa]. The shapes of these kana originate from 左 and 散, respectively.

32DB.title: Shi (kana)
32DB.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32DB.extract: Shi (hiragana: し, katakana: シ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent the phonemes /si/, reflected in the Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki romanization si, although for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [ɕi] , which is reflected in the Hepburn romanization shi. The shapes of these kana have origins in the character 之. The katakana form has become increasingly popular as an emoticon in the Western world due to its resemblance to a smiling face.

32DE.title: So (kana)
32DE.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32DE.extract: So (hiragana: そ, katakana: ソ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent [so]. Besides the one-stroke form of this kana used by computer fonts, many native Japanese writers use a different form in handwriting, here listed as an alternative form.

32DF.title: Ta (kana)
32DF.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32DF.extract: Ta (hiragana: た, katakana: タ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both represent [ta]. た originates from the Chinese character 太, while タ originates from 多.

32E0.title: Chi (kana)
32E0.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E0.extract: Chi (hiragana: ち, katakana: チ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both are phonemically /ti/, reflected in the Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki romanization ti, although, for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [t͡ɕi] , which is reflected in the Hepburn romanization chi.

32E1.title: Tsu (kana)
32E1.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E1.extract: Tsu (hiragana: つ, katakana: ツ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are phonemically /tɯ/, reflected in the Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki Romanization tu, although for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [t͡sɯᵝ] , reflected in the Hepburn romanization tsu.

32E2.title: Te (kana)
32E2.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E2.extract: Te (hiragana: て, katakana: テ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent [te].

32E3.title: To (kana)
32E3.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E3.extract: To (hiragana: と, katakana: ト) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both represent the sound [to], and when written with dakuten represent the sound [do]. In the Ainu language, the katakana ト can be written with a handakuten (which can be entered in a computer as either one character (ト゚) or two combined characters (ト゜) to represent the sound [tu], and is interchangeable with the katakana ツ゚.

32E4.title: Na (kana)
32E4.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E4.extract: Na (hiragana: な, katakana: ナ) are Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana な is made in four strokes, the katakana ナ two. Both represent [na]. な and ナ originate from the man'yōgana 奈. な is used as part of the okurigana for the plain negative forms of Japanese verbs, and several negative forms of adjectives.

32E5.title: Ni (kana)
32E5.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E5.extract: Ni (hiragana: に, katakana: ニ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is written in three strokes, while the katakana in two. Both represent /ni/ although for phonological reasons, the actual pronunciation is [ɲi].

32E6.title: Nu (kana)
32E6.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E6.extract: Nu (hiragana: ぬ, katakana: ヌ) is one of the Japanese kana each representing one mora. Both hiragana and katakana are made in two strokes and represent [nɯ]. They are both derived from the Chinese character 奴. In the Ainu language, katakana ヌ can be written as small ㇴ to represent a final n, and is interchangeable with the standard katakana ン.

32E7.title: Ne (kana)
32E7.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E7.extract: Ne (hiragana: ね, katakana: ネ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is made in two strokes, while the katakana is made in four. Both represent [ne].

32E8.title: No (kana)
32E8.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E8.extract: No (hiragana: の, katakana: ノ) are Japanese kana, both representing one mora. In the gojūon system of ordering of Japanese morae, it occupies the 25th position, between ね (ne) and は (ha). It occupies the 26th position in the iroha ordering. Both represent the sound [no]. The katakana form is written similar to the Kangxi radical 丿, radical 4.

32E9.title: Ha (kana)
32E9.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32E9.extract: Ha (hiragana: は, katakana: ハ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represent one mora. Both represent [ha]. They are also used as a grammatical particle (in such cases, they denote [wa], including in the greeting "konnichi wa") and serve as the topic marker of the sentence. は originates from 波 and ハ from 八.

32EB.title: Fu (kana)
32EB.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32EB.extract: Fu (hiragana: ふ, katakana: フ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is made in four strokes, while the katakana in one. It represents the phoneme /hɯ/, although for phonological reasons (general scheme for /h/ group, whose only phonologic survivor to /f/ ([ɸ]) remaining is ふ: b←p←f→h), the actual pronunciation is [ɸɯᵝ] , which is why it is romanized fu in Hepburn romanization instead of hu as in Nihon-shiki and Kunrei-shiki rōmaji (Korean 후 /hu/ creates the same phonetic effect as lips are projected when pronouncing "u"). Written with a dakuten (ぶ, ブ), they both represent a "bu" sound, and written with handakuten (ぷ, プ) they both represent a "pu" sound.

32EC.title: He (kana)
32EC.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32EC.extract: He (hiragana: へ, katakana: ヘ) is one of the Japanese kana, which represents one mora. The [he] sound is the only sound that is written almost identically in hiragana and katakana and therefore confusable according to the Unicode Standard. In the Sakhalin dialect of the Ainu language, ヘ can be written as small ㇸ to represent a final [h] after an [e] sound (エㇸ [eh]).

32ED.title: Ho (kana)
32ED.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32ED.extract: Ho (hiragana: ほ, katakana: ホ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are made in four strokes and both represent [ho]. In the Sakhalin dialect of the Ainu language, ホ can be written as small ㇹ to represent a final h sound after an o sound (オㇹ oh).

32EE.title: Ma (kana)
32EE.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32EE.extract: Ma (hiragana: ま, katakana: マ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is made in three strokes, while the katakana in two. Both represent [ma]. The characters ま and マ are respectively based on the sōsho style and simplification of the kanji 末.

32F0.title: Mu (kana)
32F0.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F0.extract: Mu (hiragana: む, katakana: ム) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. The hiragana is written with three strokes, while the katakana is written with two. Both represent [mɯ].

32F1.title: Me (kana)
32F1.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F1.extract: Me (hiragana: め, katakana: メ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both versions of the kana are written in two strokes and represent [me].

32F2.title: Mo (kana)
32F2.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F2.extract: Mo (hiragana: も, katakana: モ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are made in three strokes and both represent [mo].

32F3.title: Ya (kana)
32F3.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F3.extract: Ya (hiragana: や, katakana: ヤ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in three strokes, while the katakana is written in two. Both represent [ja]. Their shapes have origins in the character 也.

32F4.title: Yu (kana)
32F4.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F4.extract: Yu (hiragana: ゆ, katakana: ユ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represents one mora. Both the hiragana and katakana forms are written in two strokes and represent the sound [jɯ]. The hiragana character ゆ is based on the sōsho style of the kanji 由, while the katakana ユ is based on a simplification of the kanji 弓.

32F5.title: Yo (kana)
32F5.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F5.extract: Yo (hiragana: よ, katakana: ヨ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is made in two strokes, while the katakana in three. Both represent [jo].

32F6.title: Ra (kana)
32F6.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F6.extract: Ra (hiragana: ら; katakana: ラ) is one of the Japanese kana, which each represent one mora. Both versions are written with two strokes and have origins in the character 良; both characters represent the sound [ɾa] . The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇻ to represent a final r sound after an a sound (アㇻ ar).

32F7.title: Ri (kana)
32F7.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F7.extract: Ri (hiragana: り, katakana: リ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. Both are written with two strokes and both represent the sound [ɾi] . Both originate from the character 利. The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇼ to represent a final r sound after an i sound (イㇼ ir).

32F8.title: Ru (kana)
32F8.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F8.extract: Ru (hiragana: る, katakana: ル) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represent one mora. The hiragana is written in one stroke; the katakana in two. Both represent the sound [ɾɯ] . The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇽ to represent a final r sound after an u sound (ウㇽ ur).

32F9.title: Re (kana)
32F9.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32F9.extract: Re (hiragana: れ, katakana: レ) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in two strokes, while katakana in one. Both represent the sound [ɾe] . The shapes of these kana have origins in the character 礼. The Ainu language uses a small katakana ㇾ to represent a final r sound after an e sound (エㇾ er).

32FA.title: Ro (kana)
32FA.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32FA.extract: Ro (hiragana: ろ, katakana: ロ) (romanised as ro) is one of the Japanese kana, each of which represents one mora. The hiragana is written in one stroke, katakana in three. Both represent [ɾo] and both originate from the Chinese character 呂. The Ainu language uses a small ㇿ to represent a final r sound after an o sound (オㇿ or).

32FC.title: Wi (kana)
32FC.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32FC.extract: Wi (hiragana: ゐ, katakana: ヰ) is an obsolete kana (Japanese phonetic character) that is normally pronounced [i] (the same as the kana for i) in current-day Japanese.

32FD.title: We (kana)
32FD.description: Character of the Japanese writing system
32FD.extract: We (hiragana: ゑ, katakana: ヱ) is an obsolete kana (Japanese phonetic character) that is pronounced [e] (same pronunciation as e (kana): え) in current-day Japanese.

4DC0.extract: This is a list of the 64 hexagrams of the I Ching, or Book of Changes, and their Unicode character codes.

4E8C.title: Radical 7
4E8C.extract: Radical 7 or radical two (二部) which means "two" is one of 23 of the 214 Kangxi radicals that are composed of 2 strokes. In the Kangxi Dictionary, there are 29 characters (out of 49,030) to be found under this radical. In Simplified Chinese dictionaries and some Hong Kong Traditional Chinese dictionaries, radical 7 (radical two) is merged with radical 1 (Radical one, 一).

4EBA.title: Radical 9
4EBA.extract: Radical 9 or radical man (人部) meaning "person" is a Kangxi radical. Of the 214 radicals, Radical 9 is one of 23 which are composed of 2 strokes.

516B.title: Radical 12
516B.extract: Radical 12 or radical eight (八部), meaning eight or all, is one of 23 of the 214 Kangxi radicals that are composed of two strokes. "八" is two bent lines that signal divide. Eight is the single-digit number that can be divided by two the greatest number of times.

534D.title: Swastika
534D.description: Ancient Eurasian icon and Nazi symbol
534D.extract: The swastika ( SWOS-tih-kə, Sanskrit: [ˈsʋɐstikɐ], Sanskrit Devanagari: स्वस्तिक ; 卐 or 卍) is an ancient cross-cultural geometrical symbol that has been used in many cultures and religions of Eurasia, as well as a few in Africa and the Americas, for thousands of years. The swastika was and continues to be used as a symbol of divinity and spirituality in several religions, including Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism. In the Western world, it is predominantly associated with Nazism, being appropriated and widely displayed in Nazi symbolism. Most notably, it was used in the flag of Nazi Germany. This appropriation continues with the symbol's popularity among neo-Nazis around the world.

56CD.title: Double Happiness (calligraphy)
56CD.description: Chinese character representing wishes of happiness
56CD.extract: Double Happiness (simplified Chinese: 双喜; traditional Chinese: 雙喜; pinyin: shuāngxǐ; Vietnamese: song hỷ) sometimes translated as Double Happy, is a Chinese traditional ornament design, commonly used as a decoration symbol of marriage. Outside of China, it is also used in the United States, Europe, East Asia and Southeast Asia by members of the Overseas Chinese and Vietnamese communities.

56E7.title: Jiong
56E7.extract: Jiong (Chinese: 囧; pinyin: jiǒng; Jyutping: gwing2) is a once obscure Chinese character meaning a "patterned window". Since 2008, it has become an internet phenomenon and widely used to express embarrassment and gloom because of the character's resemblance to a sad facial expression.

58EB.title: Radical 33
58EB.extract: Radical 33 or radical scholar (士部) meaning "scholar" or "bachelor" is one of the 31 Kangxi radicals (214 radicals total) composed of three strokes.

798F.title: Fu (character)
798F.extract: The Chinese character fu (福; fú ), meaning 'fortune' or 'good luck', is represented both as a Chinese ideograph and, at times, pictorially, in one of its homophonous forms. It is often found on a figurine of the male god of the same name, one of the trio of "star gods" Fú, Lù, and Shòu.

A3E2.title: National Idea (symbol)
A3E2.extract: The National Idea (Ukrainian: Ідея нації) "ꑭ" ("ꏢ") is a symbol used by Ukrainian nationalist and Ukrainian neo-fascist organizations. It is most widely used by members of the Social-National Assembly, the Azov Civil Corps, and the Azov Brigade. The symbol has been compared with, and accused of being a variation of, the Nazi symbol Wolfsangel. The monogram is formed by intertwining these letters, with the letter "I" vertically and in the center crossing the transverse element of the letter "N".

A647.title: Iota (Cyrillic)
A647.extract: Cyrillic Iota (Majuscule: Ꙇ, Minuscule: ꙇ) is a Cyrillic letter based on the Greek letter Iota, and has been used in scholarly literature since the 10th century in the very first ie. original Cyrillic to transcribe Glagolitic izhe in its word-initial form, Ⰺ. The character was introduced into Unicode 5.1 in April 2008, under the character block Cyrillic Extended-B.

A64A.title: Uk (Cyrillic)
A64A.extract: Uk (Ѹ ѹ; italics: Ѹ ѹ) is a digraph of the early Cyrillic alphabet of the letters О and У, although commonly considered and used as a single letter. To save space, it was often written as a vertical ligature (Ꙋ ꙋ), called "monograph Uk". In modern times, ⟨оу⟩ has been replaced by the simple ⟨у⟩.

A65E.extract: Yn (Ꙟ ꙟ; italics: Ꙟ ꙟ or Ꙟ ꙟ; italics: Ꙟ ꙟ) is an archaic Cyrillic letter. It was an innovation entirely unique to the Romanian Cyrillic alphabet, not appearing in any other Cyrillic alphabet. It was derived from the Cyrillic glyph big yus.

A72A.title: Tresillo (letter)
A72A.description: Letter of several colonial Mayan alphabets in the Latin script, based on the digit 3
A72A.extract: Tresillo (capital: Ꜫ, small: ꜫ; Spanish for "little three") is a letter of several colonial Mayan alphabets in the Latin script that is based on the digit 3. It was invented by a Franciscan friar, Francisco de la Parra, in the 16th century to represent the uvular ejective consonant /qʼ/ found in Mayan languages, and is known as one of the Parra letters. In cursive form, the tresillo is often written similar to ⟨c ̑ ⟩.

A74A.title: Theta nigrum
A74A.extract: The theta nigrum (lit. 'black theta') or theta infelix (lit. 'unlucky theta') is a symbol of death in Greek and Latin epigraphy. Isidore of Seville notes the letter was appended after the name of a deceased soldier and finds of papyri containing military records have confirmed this use. Additionally it can be seen in the Gladiator Mosaic.

A74B.title: Theta nigrum
A74B.extract: The theta nigrum (lit. 'black theta') or theta infelix (lit. 'unlucky theta') is a symbol of death in Greek and Latin epigraphy. Isidore of Seville notes the letter was appended after the name of a deceased soldier and finds of papyri containing military records have confirmed this use. Additionally it can be seen in the Gladiator Mosaic.

A74C.title: O with loop
A74C.extract: O with loop (majuscule: Ꝍ, minuscule: ꝍ) is a letter used in a number of Medieval Nordic orthographies including Old Norse, Norwegian, and Icelandic. The letter was used as a scribal abbreviation during the Middle Ages to represent the phonemic /ǫ/, /ø:/, and /ey/.

A74D.title: O with loop
A74D.extract: O with loop (majuscule: Ꝍ, minuscule: ꝍ) is a letter used in a number of Medieval Nordic orthographies including Old Norse, Norwegian, and Icelandic. The letter was used as a scribal abbreviation during the Middle Ages to represent the phonemic /ǫ/, /ø:/, and /ey/.

A750.title: P
A750.description: Sixteenth letter of the Latin alphabet
A750.extract: P (minuscule: p) is the sixteenth letter of the Latin alphabet, used in the modern English alphabet, the alphabets of other western European languages and others worldwide. Its name in English is pee (pronounced ), plural pees.

A751.title: P
A751.description: Sixteenth letter of the Latin alphabet
A751.extract: P (minuscule: p) is the sixteenth letter of the Latin alphabet, used in the modern English alphabet, the alphabets of other western European languages and others worldwide. Its name in English is pee (pronounced ), plural pees.

A756.title: Q with stroke
A756.extract: Q with stroke (Ꝗ, ꝗ) is a letter of the Latin alphabet, derived from writing the letter Q with the addition of a bar through the letter's descender. The letter was used by scribes during the Middle Ages, where it was employed primarily as an abbreviation—a modern parallel of this would be abbreviating the word "and" with an ampersand (&). The letter was also used to write some modern languages. Between 1928 and 1938, the Lezgin and Dargin alphabets had used Ꝗ, but since 1938, both corresponding languages are written with Cyrillic-based alphabets, using the digraph Кь in place of Ꝗ.

A757.extract: Q with stroke (Ꝗ, ꝗ) is a letter of the Latin alphabet, derived from writing the letter Q with the addition of a bar through the letter's descender. A75A.title: R rotunda
A75A.description: Variant of the Latin letter R (ꝛ)
A75A.extract: The r rotunda ⟨ ꝛ ⟩, "rounded r", is a historical calligraphic variant of the minuscule (lowercase) letter Latin r used in full script-like typefaces, especially blackletters.

A75B.title: R rotunda
A75B.description: Variant of the Latin letter R (ꝛ)
A75B.extract: The r rotunda ⟨ ꝛ ⟩, "rounded r", is a historical calligraphic variant of the minuscule (lowercase) letter Latin r used in full script-like typefaces, especially blackletters.

A75E.title: V with diagonal stroke
A75E.extract: V with diagonal stroke (Ꝟ, ꝟ) is a letter of the Latin alphabet, derived from V with the addition of a bar through the left stroke.

A75F.title: V with diagonal stroke
A75F.extract: V with diagonal stroke (Ꝟ, ꝟ) is a letter of the Latin alphabet, derived from V with the addition of a bar through the left stroke.

A764.title: Thorn with stroke
A764.extract: Ꝥ (minuscule: ꝥ), or Þ (thorn) with stroke was a scribal abbreviation common in the Middle Ages. It was used for Old English: þæt (Modern English "that"), as well as Old Norse: þor-, the -þan/-ðan in síðan, þat, þæt, and þess. In Old English texts, the stroke tended to be more slanted, while in Old Norse texts it was straight. In Middle English times, the ascender of the þ was reduced (making it similar to the Old English letter Wynn (ƿ), which caused the thorn with stroke abbreviation ( ) to be replaced with a thorn with a small t above the letter ( ).

A765.title: Thorn with stroke
A765.extract: Ꝥ (minuscule: ꝥ), or Þ (thorn) with stroke was a scribal abbreviation common in the Middle Ages. It was used for Old English: þæt (Modern English "that"), as well as Old Norse: þor-, the -þan/-ðan in síðan, þat, þæt, and þess. A768.title: Vend (letter)
A768.extract: Vend (Ꝩ, ꝩ) is a letter of Old Norse. It was used to represent the sounds /u/, /v/, and /w/.

A769.title: Vend (letter)
A769.extract: Vend (Ꝩ, ꝩ) is a letter of Old Norse. It was used to represent the sounds /u/, /v/, and /w/.

A77D.title: Insular G
A77D.description: Form of the letter g in Insular script
A77D.extract: Insular G (majuscule: Ᵹ, minuscule: ᵹ) is a form of the letter g somewhat resembling an ezh, used in the medieval insular script of Great Britain and Ireland. It was first used in the Roman Empire in Roman cursive, then it appeared in Irish half uncial (insular) script, and after it had passed into Old English, it developed into the Middle English letter yogh (Ȝ ȝ). Middle English, having reborrowed the familiar Carolingian g from the Continent, began to use the two forms of g as separate letters.

A780.title: Turned L
A780.extract: Turned L (Ꞁ ꞁ) is an additional letter which was used in medieval Welsh and in certain phonetic transcriptions used in German dialectology. Its capital form is also homoglyphic with the letter reversed ge.

A781.title: Turned L
A781.extract: Turned L (Ꞁ ꞁ) is an additional letter which was used in medieval Welsh and in certain phonetic transcriptions used in German dialectology. Its capital form is also homoglyphic with the letter reversed ge.

A784.title: Insular S
A784.description: Insular form of the letter S (Ꞅ)
A784.extract: The letter Ꞅ (minuscule: ꞅ) is an Insular script form of the letter S. It is encoded in Unicode at U+A784 Ꞅ LATIN CAPITAL LETTER INSULAR S and U+A785 ꞅ LATIN SMALL LETTER INSULAR S.

A789.title: Colon (letter)
A789.description: Letter used in some languages for vowel length or tone
A789.extract: The colon alphabetic letter ꞉ is used in a number of languages and phonetic transcription systems, for vowel length in Americanist Phonetic Notation, for the vowels ⟨a꞉⟩ [ɛ] and ⟨o꞉⟩ [ɔ] in a number of languages of Papua New Guinea, and for grammatical tone in several languages of Africa. It resembles but differs from the colon punctuation mark, :. In some fonts, the two dots are placed a bit closer together than those of the punctuation colon so that the two characters are visually distinct.

A78D.title: Turned h
A78D.description: Additional letter of the Latin alphabet
A78D.extract: Turned H (uppercase: Ɥ, lowercase: ɥ) is an additional letter of the Latin alphabet, based on a turned form of H. It is used in the Dan language in Liberia. Its lowercase form is used in the International Phonetic Alphabet to represent the voiced labial–palatal approximant. It was also historically used in the Abaza, Abkhaz, and the Vassali Maltese alphabet.

A790.title: N with descender
A790.extract: Ꞑ, ꞑ (N with descender) is a letter of the Latin alphabet, used in several New Turkic alphabet orthographies in 1930s (for instance, Tatar alphabet), as well as in the 1990s orthographies invented in attempts to restore the Latin alphabet for the Tatar language and the Chechen language.

A791.title: N with descender
A791.extract: Ꞑ, ꞑ (N with descender) is a letter of the Latin alphabet, used in several New Turkic alphabet orthographies in 1930s (for instance, Tatar alphabet), as well as in the 1990s orthographies invented in attempts to restore the Latin alphabet for the Tatar language and the Chechen language.

A792.title: C with bar
A792.description: Additional letter of the Latin alphabet
A792.extract: Ꞓ, minuscule: ꞓ, is a modified letter of the Latin script, formed from C with the addition of a bar. It was used in the final version of the Unified Northern Alphabet, approved in 1932 for Saami, Selkup, Khanty, Evenki, Even, Nanai, Udege, Chukchi, Koryak and Nivkh languages to denote the sound [t͡ʃ], although in some of these languages in practice, several other alphabets were used. Also, this letter was used in the Latinized Shugnan alphabet (1931-1939) to denote the sound [t͡s].

A793.title: C with bar
A793.description: Additional letter of the Latin alphabet
A793.extract: Ꞓ, minuscule: ꞓ, is a modified letter of the Latin script, formed from C with the addition of a bar. It was used in the final version of the Unified Northern Alphabet, approved in 1932 for Saami, Selkup, Khanty, Evenki, Even, Nanai, Udege, Chukchi, Koryak and Nivkh languages to denote the sound [t͡ʃ], although in some of these languages in practice, several other alphabets were used. Also, this letter was used in the Latinized Shugnan alphabet (1931-1939) to denote the sound [t͡s].

A796.title: B with flourish
A796.description: Letter of the Latin alphabet used in Middle Vietnamese
A796.extract: B with flourish (Ꞗ, ꞗ) is the Unicode name for the third letter of the Middle Vietnamese alphabet, sorted between B and C. The B with flourish has a rounded hook that starts halfway up the stem (where the top of the bowl meets the ascender) and curves about 180 degrees counterclockwise, ending below the bottom-left corner. It represents the voiced bilabial fricative /β/, which in modern Vietnamese merged with the voiced labiodental fricative, written as the letter V in the Vietnamese alphabet. (In Middle Vietnamese, V represented the labio-velar approximant /w/.)

A797.title: B with flourish
A797.description: Letter of the Latin alphabet used in Middle Vietnamese
A797.extract: B with flourish (Ꞗ, ꞗ) is the Unicode name for the third letter of the Middle Vietnamese alphabet, sorted between B and C. The B with flourish has a rounded hook that starts halfway up the stem (where the top of the bowl meets the ascender) and curves about 180 degrees counterclockwise, ending below the bottom-left corner. It represents the voiced bilabial fricative /β/, which in modern Vietnamese merged with the voiced labiodental fricative, written as the letter V in the Vietnamese alphabet. (In Middle Vietnamese, V represented the labio-velar approximant /w/.)

A79E.title: Ꞟ
A79E.extract: Ꞟ (minuscule: ꞟ) was an additional letter of the Latin alphabet that was used in the writing of Volapük in the 19th century. It is now transcribed ⟨Ü ü⟩ in Volapük.

A79F.title: Ꞟ
A79F.extract: Ꞟ (minuscule: ꞟ) was an additional letter of the Latin alphabet that was used in the writing of Volapük in the 19th century. It is now transcribed ⟨Ü ü⟩ in Volapük.

A7A0.title: G with oblique stroke
A7A0.description: Letter of the extended Latin alphabet
A7A0.extract: Ꞡ (lowercase ꞡ) is a letter derived from the Latin alphabet letter G, combined with an oblique bar diacritic. It was used in Latvian orthography before 1921. Karl Faulmann reported in 1880 that the character was used to indicate a "g lind" (i.e., a soft g, the voiced post-alveolar affricate [d͡ʒ]), as opposed to the "hard g" that was denoted by a regular g character.

A7A1.description: Letter of the extended Latin alphabet
A7A1.extract: Ꞡ (lowercase ꞡ) is a letter derived from the Latin alphabet letter G, combined with an oblique bar diacritic. It was used in Latvian orthography before 1921. A7A2.title: Ꞣ
A7A2.extract: Ꞣ (lowercase ꞣ) is a letter of the Latin script, composed of the letter K with an oblique stroke. It was used in Latvian before 1921, where it was replaced with Ķ.

A7A3.title: Ꞣ
A7A3.extract: Ꞣ (lowercase ꞣ) is a letter of the Latin script, composed of the letter K with an oblique stroke. It was used in Latvian before 1921, where it was replaced with Ķ.

A7A4.title: N with oblique stroke
A7A4.extract: Ꞥ (lowercase ꞥ) is a letter derived from the combination of the Latin letter N and a stroke diacritic. Until 1921, it was used in Latvian orthography to represent the hard palatal nasal /ɲ/. It was replaced by Ņ (N with a cedilla).

A7A5.title: N with oblique stroke
A7A5.extract: Ꞥ (lowercase ꞥ) is a letter derived from the combination of the Latin letter N and a stroke diacritic. Until 1921, it was used in Latvian orthography to represent the hard palatal nasal /ɲ/. It was replaced by Ņ (N with a cedilla).

A7A6.title: R with oblique stroke
A7A6.extract: Ꞧ (lowercase ꞧ) is a letter derived from the Latin alphabet letter R, combined with bar diacritic.

A7A7.title: R with oblique stroke
A7A7.extract: Ꞧ (lowercase ꞧ) is a letter derived from the Latin alphabet letter R, combined with bar diacritic.

A7A8.title: S with oblique stroke
A7A8.extract: Ꞩ, ꞩ, ẜ (S with oblique stroke) is an extended Latin letter that was used in Latvian orthography until 1921; ꞩ was also used in Lower Sorbian until 1950. A variant of the letter S with a stroke, encoded at U+A7CC Ꟍ LATIN CAPITAL LETTER S WITH DIAGONAL STROKE and U+A7CD ꟍ LATIN SMALL LETTER S WITH DIAGONAL STROKE, is used in Luiseño and Cupeño,

A variant of the letter S with a stroke, encoded at U+A7CC Ꟍ LATIN CAPITAL LETTER S WITH DIAGONAL STROKE and U+A7CD ꟍ LATIN SMALL LETTER S WITH DIAGONAL STROKE, is used in Luiseño and Cupeño,

A7AE.title: Small capital I
A7AE.description: Additional letter of the Latin alphabet
A7AE.extract: Small capital I is an additional letter of the Latin alphabet similar in its dimensions to the Latin letter "I" but with a shape based on ⟨I⟩, its capital form. Although ⟨ɪ⟩ is usually an allograph of the Latin letter I i, it is considered as an additional letter in the African reference alphabet and has been used as such in some publications in the Kulango languages in Côte d'Ivoire in the 1990s. In the International Phonetic Alphabet, the lowercase small capital I /ɪ/ is used as the symbol for the near-close near-front unrounded vowel, like the letter i in the word "fit".

A7B4.title: Latin beta
A7B4.description: Additional letter of the Latin alphabet
A7B4.extract: Latin beta (uppercase: Ꞵ, lowercase: ꞵ), is an additional letter of the Latin script. Its shape is based on the lowercase shape of the Greek letter beta ⟨β⟩. The letter is used in the various languages of Gabon and has been used in Ndaʼndaʼ language in Cameroon to represent the voiced bilabial fricative, a sound similar to ⟨v⟩ articulated with both lips. It is neither typographically nor linguistically related to the similar looking letter eszett ⟨ẞ, ß⟩ used in German orthography, which represents an /s/ sound when following long vowels or diphthongs.

A7B5.title: Latin beta
A7B5.description: Additional letter of the Latin alphabet
A7B5.extract: Latin beta (uppercase: Ꞵ, lowercase: ꞵ), is an additional letter of the Latin script. Its shape is based on the lowercase shape of the Greek letter beta ⟨β⟩. The letter is used in the various languages of Gabon and has been used in Ndaʼndaʼ language in Cameroon to represent the voiced bilabial fricative, a sound similar to ⟨v⟩ articulated with both lips. It is neither typographically nor linguistically related to the similar looking letter eszett ⟨ẞ, ß⟩ used in German orthography, which represents an /s/ sound when following long vowels or diphthongs.

A7B6.title: Latin omega
A7B6.extract: Latin omega, or simply omega, is an additional letter of the Latin alphabet, based on the lowercase shape of the Greek letter omega ⟨ω⟩. It was included as a Latin letter in the Mann and Dalby 1982 revision of the African Reference Alphabet and has been used as such in some publications in the Kulango languages in Côte d'Ivoire in the 1990s. In other Kulango publications the letters V with hook ⟨Ʋ⟩ or Latin upsilon ⟨Ʊ⟩ are found instead.

A7B7.title: Latin omega
A7B7.extract: Latin omega, or simply omega, is an additional letter of the Latin alphabet, based on the lowercase shape of the Greek letter omega ⟨ω⟩. It was included as a Latin letter in the Mann and Dalby 1982 revision of the African Reference Alphabet and has been used as such in some publications in the Kulango languages in Côte d'Ivoire in the 1990s. In other Kulango publications the letters V with hook ⟨Ʋ⟩ or Latin upsilon ⟨Ʊ⟩ are found instead.

A7B8.title: U
A7B8.description: Twenty-first letter of the Latin alphabet
A7B8.extract: U (minuscule: u) is the twenty-first letter and the fifth vowel letter of the Latin alphabet, used in the modern English alphabet and the alphabets of other western European languages and others worldwide. Its name in English is u (pronounced ), plural ues.

A7B9.title: U
A7B9.description: Twenty-first letter of the Latin alphabet
A7B9.extract: U (minuscule: u) is the twenty-first letter and the fifth vowel letter of the Latin alphabet, used in the modern English alphabet and the alphabets of other western European languages and others worldwide. Its name in English is u (pronounced ), plural ues.

A7C7.title: Tau gallicum
A7C7.extract: Tau gallicum (majuscule: Ꟈ (), minuscule: ꟈ ()) is a letter that was used by the Gauls in their language. It is a D with the horizontal bar from the Greek letter theta (Θ). It likely represented a /t͡s/ or /st/ sound, like the ts in cats or the st in stop, though gemination is seldom present, such as in the Chamalières tablet.

A7C8.title: Tau gallicum
A7C8.extract: Tau gallicum (majuscule: Ꟈ (), minuscule: ꟈ ()) is a letter that was used by the Gauls in their language. It is a D with the horizontal bar from the Greek letter theta (Θ). It likely represented a /t͡s/ or /st/ sound, like the ts in cats or the st in stop, though gemination is seldom present, such as in the Chamalières tablet.

A7CB.title: Ram's horn (letter)
A7CB.extract: Ram's horn (majuscule: Ɤ, minuscule: ɤ) is a letter of the extended Latin alphabet used in the International Phonetic Alphabet to transcribe a close-mid back unrounded vowel, and in the 2014 Eastern Dan orthography and the 2020 Goo orthography in Cote d'Ivoire.

A7D8.title: Sigmoid S
A7D8.description: Middle English variant of the letter S
A7D8.extract: Sigmoid S (Ꟙ ꟙ) is a letter of the Latin script that was commonly used in Middle English, Middle Scots, and Middle Cornish.

A7D9.title: Sigmoid S
A7D9.description: Middle English variant of the letter S
A7D9.extract: Sigmoid S (Ꟙ ꟙ) is a letter of the Latin script that was commonly used in Middle English, Middle Scots, and Middle Cornish.

A7F5.title: Reversed half H
A7F5.extract: The reversed half H (Ꟶ or ꟶ) was a letter used in Latin inscriptions from Roman Gaul. In French epigraphy works, it is called H dimidiée, "halved H".

A7F7.title: Sideways I
A7F7.description: Epigraphic letter of the Latin alphabet
A7F7.extract: The Sideways I ꟷ is an epigraphic variant of Latin capital letter I used in early medieval Celtic inscriptions from Wales and southwest England (Cornwall and Devon). About 36 monumental inscriptions in Wales, and about 15 in Cornwall and Devon, mostly dating from the 5th-6th centuries, make use of this letter. Except for a single inscription from the Isle of Man, it is not found in monumental inscriptions elsewhere. The letter is used exclusively in a word-final position for Latin words (or Latinized Celtic names) in the second declension genitive singular.

A7FB.title: Reversed F
A7FB.extract: Reversed F (ꟻ f ) is an additional Latin script letter used in epigraphic inscriptions to abbreviate the words filia or femina. It was also formerly used in the writing of the Abaza, the Abkhaz, the Adyghe and the Kabardian languages in the 1920s and 1930s.

A7FE.title: Long I
A7FE.extract: Long i (Latin: i longum or [littera] i longa), written ⟨ꟾ⟩, is a variant of the letter i found in ancient and early medieval forms of the Latin script.

AB36.title: Cross-tailed G
AB36.description: Letter of the Latin alphabet, a phonetic symbol
AB36.extract: ꬶ (lowercase only) is a letter of the Latin alphabet.

E000.title: Private Use Areas
E000.extract: In Unicode, the Private Use Areas (PUA) are three blocks that are not assigned characters by the standard. The three blocks are Private Use Area, in the Basic Multilingual Plane (U+E000–U+F8FF), Supplementary Private Use Area-A and Supplementary Private Use Area-B, the latter two being in and covering nearly all of planes 15 and 16 (U+F0000–U+FFFFD, U+100000–U+10FFFD), respectively. They are intentionally left undefined so that third parties may assign their own characters without conflicting with Unicode Standard assignments. Under the Unicode Stability Policy, the Private Use Areas will remain allocated for that purpose in all future Unicode versions.
